marble.name: Lines of symmetry
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry
marble.prompt: If you show you half a shape drawn on squared paper with a mirror line marked, can they draw the missing half so the whole shape is perfectly symmetrical?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring shapes and space — recognising circles, triangles, and squares, building with 3D shapes like cubes and spheres, and describing where things are using words like above, below, and beside.

misconceptions: Completing the figure by eye so the reflected points are not equidistant from the mirror line.
Sliding a copy of the half across (translating) rather than reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image.
Miscounting the squares, so individual partner points land the wrong distance from the mirror.
Duplicating or shifting points that lie on the mirror line instead of leaving them fixed.
representations: Squared grid with a marked mirror line and the given half of the figure
Perpendicular counting arrows from each point of the given half to its partner on the far side
Fold test / Mira mirror placed on the line to verify the halves coincide
Butterfly or letter half as an intuitive 'complete the other side' context
authoredAnswer: The child builds the missing half point by point — each partner point the same number of squares perpendicular from the mirror line as its original, joined in the same order — so the completed figure is a true mirror image (sense reversed), leaves any on-the-line points fixed, and works for the horizontal mirror as well as the vertical. wrongAnswers.revealedBy: The second half is drawn freehand and roughly opposite; partner points are the wrong distance out; a fold would not line up.
wrongAnswers.fix: Return to counting: for each point, count squares perpendicular to the mirror and mark the same count on the far side; then fold to confirm. Revisit what a line of symmetry means.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: The two halves face the SAME way (a butterfly's wings both point right); sense is not reversed even if the copy is neatly placed.
wrongAnswers.fix: Show the fold does not match; rebuild one feature by the perpendicular-equidistant rule so the reversal emerges. Contrast 'reflect' with 'slide'.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Most of the figure is correct but one or two points are a square off; the overall shape is nearly right and the child is surprised when the fold misses there.
wrongAnswers.fix: Do not reteach reflection — have the child re-count the slipped point, marking the perpendicular squares on both sides, and fold to self-correct.

before.name: 2-D shapes (age 8+)
before.reason: Softened (Ontario G1 readiness review): Completing a figure about a given mirror line needs basic line symmetry, not all lines of symmetry in rotated or regular shapes.

before.name: 2-D shapes (age 6+)
before.reason: Basic prerequisite (Ontario G1 readiness review): Identifying a vertical line of symmetry is the real prerequisite.

before.reason: Softened (Ontario G1 readiness review): Full grid transformations are not needed to complete a simple symmetric figure; checking is by folding.
